narrative:
The model predicts you have a 25% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to strengthen your chances of success.

The three factors that most strongly shaped this prediction were your number of past class failures, your desire to pursue higher education, and the size of your family. Surprisingly, having no previous failures was the strongest element pulling the prediction toward passing. Your clear ambition to continue studying beyond high school also pushed the outcome in a positive direction. However, coming from a smaller family worked against you and was the main reason the model still saw a notable risk of failure.

Students from smaller families appear to face extra challenges in this dataset, possibly because they receive less peer support at home compared with the majority of students who passed and came from larger households. In your case, this factor outweighed the protective effects of your clean failure record and strong educational goals.

To improve, focus on building consistent daily study habits beyond the less-than-two hours you currently spend, since most successful students dedicate more time. Consider reaching out to teachers for extra guidance, making better use of your internet access for learning resources, and cutting back on weekend socialising and alcohol consumption that may be quietly affecting your concentration. Small, steady changes in these areas can meaningfully raise your odds of passing.
